2: (a) This question asked candidates to identify and explain two reasons why employees might want to join a trade union. Many answers discussed the benefits that could be negotiated, such as improved working conditions, more holidays and fewer working hours. The highest credit for this response was, as always, given to candidates who successfully related their explanation to the car company in the case study rather than provide a generic answer. Only strong candidates gained full marks by fully applying their analysis to this business in the case but many did gain application marks in both sections for identifying the problems for the employees at this company as outlined in the case. Weaker candidates often did not explain how the trade union could help improve these issues for workers, such as there being strength in numbers being more effective in pressuring for improvements. (b) This question was concerned with the effects on SC of three factors when considering the marketing of its cars in foreign markets. Many candidates identified higher levels of competition as being a problem but then only stronger candidates went onto explain how this would affect the marketing in the foreign market. Consumer needs was often the best answered of the factors with candidates arguing that if the car did not meet customer needs then it would not be successful and that market research might be needed before entering the market to ensure customer needs were identified. 3: (a) This question was well answered by the majority of candidates. Candidates often gave answers that recognised making cars to the exact requirements of customers would meet customer needs, encourage brand loyalty and lead to word-of-mouth advertising to family and friends of customers. These answers were often well applied by referring to the cars meeting customer needs but only stronger candidates gained both application marks. Many answers recognised that producing cars to the exact requirements of customers would increase costs and take time to read the bar codes and adjust equipment to make a slightly different car each time. However, most candidates scored less than full marks due to a lack of full application to the case. (b) This was one of the less well-answered questions on the paper. Many candidates lacked knowledge of the different methods of ensuring quality even if they could name quality control, quality assurance or Total Quality Management. Only a few recognised that SC was already using quality control and if they did they often could not explain how it could be used. There were confused answers that discussed consumers’ test driving the cars and feeding back information to SC. There also seemed to be a lot of confusion between quality control and quality assurance and how they are carried out. 4: (a) Many candidates gained at least four marks if not more for this question as they could identify methods such as letters, email, text messages, advertising or posters, telephone/mobile phone or noticeboards. The majority of candidates could then go on to explain when these methods might be used, such as telephone to contact suppliers of tyres. (b) Many candidates scored well by calculating the gross profit, (net) profit and ROCE ratios for both years. Better candidates identified in the recommendation that the business had the same gross profit and (net) profit for both years and had therefore not increased either of these. However, there were lower profitability ratios for all three ratios. Candidates argued that SC is less likely to pay increased dividends in the future and is therefore not worth investing in. Weaker answers just considered what was happening to the figures, e.g. for example revenue increased by $50m or incorrectly calculated the ratios. Few candidates applied their answers to the business in the case and therefore few candidates gained full marks. Where application was awarded it tended to be for identifying the longer term trends in car sales as outlined in Appendix 3 leading to the possibility of increased sales and profit for SC in the future.
